title: A two-minute breath
intro: A short reset you can do anywhere. Follow along at your own pace.

blocks.text: Sit comfortably. Let your shoulders drop away from your ears.
Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four.
Let it out gently through your mouth for a count of six.
Notice the air moving in and out. There's nowhere else to be right now.
If your mind wanders, that's fine. Just guide it gently back to the breath.
Take one more slow breath, and let it go.
You just gave your nervous system a moment of calm. That's a skill, and you're practising it.

title: Making room for the urge
intro: An acceptance practice. Instead of fighting the urge, you make space for it — and watch it lose its grip.

blocks.text: Notice the urge is here. You don't have to like it. You just have to notice it.
Where do you feel it in your body? Your chest, your stomach, your hands?
Breathe into that place. Imagine making a little more room around the feeling.
You are the sky. The urge is just weather passing through. Storms don't damage the sky.
You don't have to push the urge away, and you don't have to act on it. Both take energy. Just let it be here.
Watch it the way you'd watch a wave. Rising… cresting… and beginning to fall.
Urges always pass. You didn't fight this one — you let it move through. That's the harder, stronger skill.

title: A self-compassion break
intro: Three short steps, based on the work of Kristin Neff, for the moments you're being hard on yourself.

blocks.text: First, acknowledge it: 'This is a moment of struggle.' Naming pain is the start of easing it.
Second, remember you're not alone: 'Struggle is part of being human. Many people feel exactly this.'
Third, offer yourself some kindness. Put a hand on your chest if it helps.
Say to yourself: 'May I be kind to myself. May I give myself the compassion I need.'
Talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a good friend who was struggling. You deserve that same warmth.
Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook — it's what actually makes change possible. Shame keeps the loop spinning; kindness quiets it.

title: Loving-kindness
intro: A gentle practice of goodwill — toward yourself and others. It softens the isolation that urges feed on.

blocks.text: Settle in and take a slow breath.
Bring yourself to mind. Silently offer: 'May I be well. May I be at ease. May I be kind to myself.'
Now bring to mind someone you care about. Offer them the same: 'May you be well. May you be at ease.'
Widen it to someone you feel neutral about — a stranger you passed today. 'May you be well too.'
And finally, to everyone also trying to change something hard: 'May we all find our way.'
Notice how it feels to wish others well. Connection and warmth are the opposite of the loop.
